models_evaluated: 72 LLMs (proprietary and open-weight, including medical fine-tuned models)

links.outcome: Rate of LLMs following harmful or prohibited instructions (violation rate) in robotic health attendant simulation
links.effect: Mean violation rate across 72 LLMs was 54.4%, with more than half of models exceeding 50%; proprietary median 23.7% vs open-weight 72.8%.
links.quote: The mean violation rate across all models was 54.4\%, with more than half exceeding 50\%, and violation rates varied substantially across behavior categories, with superficially plausible instructions such as device manipulation and emergency delay proving harder to refuse than overtly destructive ones.

links.outcome: Agent LLM execution of harmful actions outside its safe envelope in simulated robot control
links.effect: Mean violation rate 54.4% across 72 LLMs; device manipulation and emergency delay instructions harder to refuse than overtly destructive ones.
links.quote: The mean violation rate across all models was 54.4\%, with more than half exceeding 50\%, and violation rates varied substantially across behavior categories, with superficially plausible instructions such as device manipulation and emergency delay proving harder to refuse than overtly destructive ones.

links.outcome: Whether medical domain fine-tuning improved safety on harmful instruction refusal
links.effect: Medical domain fine-tuning conferred no significant overall safety benefit.
links.quote: Medical domain fine-tuning conferred no significant overall safety benefit, and a prompt-based defense strategy produced only a modest reduction in violation rates among the least safe models, leaving absolute violation rates at levels that would preclude safe clinical deployment.

unlisted_practices: Prompt-based defense strategy (safety system prompt) to reduce violations
